# On Tide Tables

There is a small booklet, usually free at harbor offices and bait shops, that I find quietly astonishing. It is the tide table: rows of times and heights, printed in a font that has not been fashionable since the 1990s, listing when the sea will rise and fall at some particular spot on the coast. High water at 6:42 a.m., 6.1 feet. Low water at 12:55 p.m., 0.4 feet. And so on, for every day of the year, months before any of those days have happened.

We don't usually find this remarkable because we are used to prediction. Weather apps now tell us it will rain at 3:15, and we treat this as ordinary until the rain arrives at 3:40 and we feel betrayed. But the tide table doesn't hedge. It doesn't say "60% chance of high water." The ocean is not being forecast so much as *understood*, and that is a different relationship altogether.

The tides are, after all, the result of a conversation between bodies that are unimaginably far apart. The moon pulls on the water, the sun pulls on it a little less, and the rotating Earth drags its oceans through these gravitational gradients like a hand through a bathtub. Add in the shape of the coastline, the depth of the seabed, the width of the bay, and the way water sloshes back and forth in a basin like soup in a bowl, and you get a local rhythm that is unique to each place. The high tide in one harbor can be hours off from the next harbor over. A tide table for a given port is therefore a kind of portrait: a distillation of everything about that spot's relationship to the cosmos.

And people worked this out mostly by paying attention. Long before anyone could write the equations, fishermen and pilots noticed that the tides ran later each day by roughly fifty minutes, that they swelled at the new and full moon and softened at the quarters. They kept records. Harbor masters passed along notes. Eventually, mathematicians like Laplace and later Kelvin realized that the tide at any place could be broken into a sum of many simple waves, each tied to some periodic motion of the moon or sun: one for the moon's orbit, one for its varying distance, one for the sun's apparent path, and dozens more. Kelvin even built a machine, a brass-and-wire contraption of pulleys and dials, that added up these waves mechanically and drew the tide curve on paper. It was an analog computer for the sea.

I love that. A machine made of gears that hums along in sympathy with the moon.

What moves me most, though, is not the cleverness. It is the humility built into the whole enterprise. A tide table doesn't try to control the sea, or even to explain it to you. It says: here is when it will come, here is when it will go, plan accordingly. It is an act of fitting yourself to the world instead of fitting the world to yourself. The person who reads the table and decides to walk out to the sandbar at low water, and to be back before the flood, is participating in an old bargain. The sea keeps its schedule; you keep yours in relation to it.

There's a certain kind of modern life that has forgotten how to make this bargain. Much of what surrounds us is designed to be available at any time: light at midnight, strawberries in January, answers at any hour. This is wonderful in many ways, and I wouldn't trade it for a candle and a root cellar. But it does mean we rarely experience the world as having rhythms we must yield to. The tide is one of the last things that flatly refuses to be on demand. You cannot request low tide. You can only find out when it is coming and show up.

I suspect this is why standing at the edge of a tidal flat feels the way it does. There is something a little vertiginous about watching a whole landscape appear and disappear on a schedule. Mud, rocks, and the skeletons of old pilings emerge, gleaming, and for a few hours the place is a different place. Crabs rearrange themselves. Birds arrive in their hundreds, probing the wet sand with beaks shaped precisely for that purpose. Then, without any drama, the water begins to return, first as thin silver threads in the low channels and then as a steady advance, and the whole scene is quietly erased. Nobody announces it. If you weren't paying attention, you would swear the water had always been there.

The tide table is the thing that lets you be paying attention. It is a promise from the past to the future: someone did the arithmetic, so you don't have to be surprised.

I think there's a broader lesson here about what knowledge is *for*. We tend to celebrate discovery, the dramatic moment when someone sees something new. But a huge portion of human knowledge is more like the tide table: dull-looking, useful, patient, quietly averting disaster every day. The bridge-load chart. The seed-planting calendar. The dosage guide. The list of which mushrooms will kill you. None of these will ever have a movie made about them, and yet a civilization is largely built out of such documents. They are how the hard-won attention of one generation becomes the ordinary safety of the next.

I sometimes imagine a person, centuries from now, finding one of these booklets in a drawer, faded and water-stained, and trying to work out what it meant. They would see the columns of numbers and might guess at the truth: that here was a people who watched the sea closely enough to predict it, and who cared enough about one another to write it down. That the times and heights were not just data but a kind of kindness, offered to strangers who hadn't yet arrived at the shore.

It's not a bad thing to be remembered for. *High water at 6:42. Mind the flood.*

Next time you pass a harbor office, take a booklet. They're usually free. Keep it in a drawer or a glove compartment. Even if you never walk out onto a sandbar, it's a pleasant thing to own: a small, printed reminder that the world keeps time, that some of its clocks are enormous and wet and lunar, and that a person with a pencil and enough patience can learn to read them.
